facts.summary: American theorist of neoliberal institutionalism and, with Joseph Nye, of complex interdependence.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Joseph Nye
facts.summary: American liberal scholar of international relations who coined soft power and, with Keohane, developed complex interdependence.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Alexander Wendt
facts.summary: American constructivist who argued that anarchy and power politics are shaped by the identities states construct.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Immanuel Wallerstein
facts.summary: American sociologist who founded world-systems theory.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: David Mitrany
facts.summary: Romanian-born British scholar who founded functionalism in international relations.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Samuel Huntington
facts.summary: American political scientist known for the clash of civilizations thesis and for work on political order and democratisation.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Francis Fukuyama
facts.summary: American political scientist who argued that the triumph of liberal democracy after the Cold War marked the end of history.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Woodrow Wilson
facts.summary: US President whose Fourteen Points and League of Nations shaped the idealist approach to international relations.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Sir Syed Ahmad Khan
facts.summary: Muslim reformer who urged modern education and loyalty to British rule and founded the Muhammadan Anglo-Oriental College at Aligarh.
facts.note: IGNOU gives 1817-1898 in one unit and 1817-99 in another.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Sri Aurobindo
facts.summary: Extremist nationalist turned spiritual philosopher who saw the nation as divine and set out the doctrine of passive resistance.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Mahatma Gandhi
facts.summary: Leader of the national movement whose thought rests on truth, non-violence, satyagraha, swaraj and trusteeship.
facts.verified: books: Heywood; IGNOU Political Science Paper 2

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: B. R. Ambedkar
facts.summary: Dalit leader and chair of the Drafting Committee who fought caste through law, rights and social democracy.
facts.note: IGNOU gives 14 April 1891; Austin's Constituent Assembly table prints 1893.
facts.verified: books: Austin; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: M. N. Roy
facts.summary: Early Indian communist who broke with Marxism and founded radical humanism.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Jawaharlal Nehru
facts.summary: First Prime Minister of India, who shaped non-alignment, Panchsheel and planned development.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: A. R. Desai
facts.summary: Indian Marxist sociologist who explained nationalism through the economic and class changes of colonial rule.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Granville Austin
facts.summary: American historian of the Indian Constitution, who called it first and foremost a social document.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: K. C. Wheare
facts.summary: Australian-born constitutional scholar who defined the federal principle and called the Indian Constitution quasi-federal.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Republic
facts.summary: Dialogue that defines justice as each of three classes doing its own work, with philosopher-kings ruling the ideal state.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Politics
facts.summary: Treatise that classifies constitutions by who rules and for whose good, and favours polity as the best practicable state.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Arthashastra
facts.summary: Treatise on statecraft, economy and diplomacy covering the seven limbs of the state, the duties of the king and the circle of states.
facts.note: Its date is debated; tradition places it in the 4th century BCE, many scholars later.
facts.verified: books: Baylis & Smith; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Prince
facts.summary: Advice to a new prince on gaining and holding power, using force and deceit when needed.
facts.note: Written in 1513 and printed after his death in 1532; books cite both years.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Leviathan
facts.summary: Argues that people in a state of nature, a war of all against all, contract to obey an absolute sovereign who keeps the peace.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Two Treatises of Government
facts.summary: Rejects divine-right monarchy and grounds limited government in consent, to protect life, liberty and property.
facts.note: Printed in late 1689 with 1690 on the title page; books cite both years.
facts.verified: books: Heywood; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Social Contract
facts.summary: Holds that legitimate authority comes from a contract that makes the people sovereign under the general will.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: On Liberty
facts.summary: Defends freedom of thought, expression and action, allowing interference only to prevent harm to others.
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Political Science Paper 1; O.P. Gauba

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Communist Manifesto
facts.summary: Pamphlet declaring that all history is the history of class struggles and calling on workers to overthrow capitalism.
facts.note: Co-written with Friedrich Engels.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Imperialism, the Highest Stage of Capitalism
aliases: Imperialism: The Highest Stage of Capitalism
facts.summary: Explains imperialism as monopoly capitalism that exports capital and divides the world among the great powers.
facts.note: Written in 1916, published in 1917.
facts.verified: books: Baylis & Smith; Heywood; O.P. Gauba

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Prison Notebooks
facts.summary: Notes written in a fascist prison that develop hegemony, civil and political society, passive revolution and organic intellectuals.
facts.note: Written 1929-1935 and published after his death: in Italian from 1948, in an English selection in 1971.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Origins of Totalitarianism
facts.summary: Traces Nazi and Stalinist totalitarianism to antisemitism, imperialism and mass society, and to rule by terror and ideology.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: A Theory of Justice
facts.summary: Derives two principles of justice, equal basic liberties and inequalities only to the benefit of the least advantaged, from an original position.
facts.verified: books: Heywood; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Anarchy, State, and Utopia
facts.summary: Defends a minimal state and an entitlement theory: holdings justly acquired or transferred are just, so redistribution violates rights.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Idea of Justice
facts.summary: Rejects the search for a perfectly just society and compares real outcomes, contrasting niti with nyaya.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Spheres of Justice
facts.summary: Argues for complex equality, in which each social good is distributed within its own sphere by its own social meaning.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Two Concepts of Liberty
facts.summary: Lecture that separates negative liberty from positive liberty and warns that positive liberty can be used to justify coercion.
facts.note: Oxford inaugural lecture of 1958, reprinted in Four Essays on Liberty in 1969.
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Political Science Paper 1; O.P. Gauba

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Capitalism, Socialism and Democracy
facts.summary: Redefines democracy as a method in which leaders gain power by competing for the people's vote.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Political System
facts.summary: Calls for a general theory of politics and defines politics as the authoritative allocation of values for a society.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Civic Culture
facts.summary: Five-nation survey that sorts political culture into parochial, subject and participant types and links a mixed civic culture to stable democracy.
facts.note: Co-written with Sidney Verba.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Power: A Radical View
facts.summary: Argues that power has three dimensions: decision-making, agenda-setting, and shaping people's wants and beliefs.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Road to Serfdom
facts.summary: Warns that central economic planning leads to the loss of freedom and to totalitarianism.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: A Grammar of Politics
facts.summary: Argues for a pluralist state that shares authority with associations and treats rights as the conditions of self-development.
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Political Science Paper 1; O.P. Gauba

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Second Sex
facts.summary: Argues that one is not born but becomes a woman, as society makes woman man's Other.
facts.note: French original 1949, English translation 1953.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Politics Among Nations
facts.summary: Classical realist text holding that international politics is a struggle for power and that states act on interest defined as power.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Twenty Years' Crisis, 1919-1939
facts.summary: Criticises interwar utopianism and argues that sound thinking about world politics must combine realism and utopia.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Theory of International Politics
facts.summary: Founds neorealism: anarchy and the distribution of capabilities shape state behaviour, and a bipolar system is the most stable.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Tragedy of Great Power Politics
facts.summary: Sets out offensive realism: in anarchy great powers maximise relative power and aim at regional hegemony.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Power and Interdependence
facts.summary: Sets out complex interdependence against realism: multiple channels between societies, no hierarchy of issues and a minor role for military force.
facts.note: Co-written with Joseph Nye.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Anarchy is What States Make of It
facts.summary: Article arguing that self-help and power politics do not follow from anarchy but from identities and interests that states construct.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The End of History and the Last Man
facts.summary: Argues that liberal democracy may be the end point of humanity's ideological evolution.
facts.note: Grew out of his 1989 essay 'The End of History?' in The National Interest.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Hind Swaraj
facts.summary: Dialogue that condemns modern Western civilisation and defines true swaraj as self-rule through non-violence.
facts.note: Written in Gujarati in 1909; the English translation appeared in 1910.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Annihilation of Caste
facts.summary: Undelivered speech that attacks caste and its basis in the Hindu shastras and calls for its destruction.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Causes of the Indian Revolt
facts.summary: Argues that the revolt of 1857 arose because the British misunderstood Indians and kept them out of the Legislative Council.
facts.note: Written in 1858 and published in 1859; books cite both years.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Doctrine of Passive Resistance
facts.summary: Articles arguing for organised passive resistance through boycott and swadeshi, while allowing force against violent repression.
facts.note: First published as articles in Bande Mataram in 1907.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Social Background of Indian Nationalism
facts.summary: Marxist account of Indian nationalism as a product of the economic and class changes brought by British rule.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation
facts.summary: History of the Constituent Assembly showing how it built the Constitution through consensus and accommodation.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Philosopher-king
facts.summary: Plato's ideal ruler, who knows the Good through reason and rules the just state without private property or family.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Saptanga theory
facts.summary: Kautilya's theory that the state has seven elements: swami, amatya, janapada, durga, kosha, danda and mitra.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Mandala theory
facts.summary: Kautilya's circle of states, in which a neighbouring state is a natural enemy and the state beyond it a natural ally.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Dharmashastra
facts.summary: Brahmanical texts such as the Manusmriti that make protecting dharma and the varna order the king's duty, or rajadharma.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Mahasammata
facts.summary: Buddhist idea, from the Agganna Sutta, that the people chose the first king to keep order: an early contract theory.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Sovereignty
facts.summary: Supreme and final legal authority of the state over its territory and people, systematised by Bodin and developed by Hobbes and Austin.
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Political Science Paper 1; O.P. Gauba

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: General will
facts.summary: Rousseau's idea of the will of the sovereign people aimed at the common good, as distinct from the will of all.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Harm principle
facts.summary: Mill's principle that power may be used over anyone against their will only to prevent harm to others.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Historical materialism
facts.summary: Marx's view that the mode of production is the base on which law, politics and ideas rise as a superstructure.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Hegemony
facts.summary: Gramsci's idea that a ruling class rules by winning the consent of the ruled through civil society, not by force alone.
facts.note: In IR the word also means a dominant state's leadership, which is not Gramsci's sense.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Three types of authority
facts.summary: Weber's three types of legitimate domination: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational authority.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Negative and positive liberty
facts.summary: Berlin's distinction between freedom from interference by others and freedom as self-mastery or self-rule.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Original position
facts.summary: Rawls's hypothetical choice in which people pick principles of justice behind a veil of ignorance about their own place in society.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Capability approach
facts.summary: Judges well-being and justice by what people are actually able to do and to be, not by income or resources alone.
facts.note: Also developed by Martha Nussbaum.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Polyarchy
facts.summary: Dahl's term for real-world democracies, marked by wide participation and open public contestation among competing groups.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Deliberative democracy
facts.summary: Model in which democratic legitimacy comes from free and equal public reasoning among citizens, not only from voting.
facts.note: Joseph Bessette coined the term in 1980; Habermas is its leading theorist.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Behaviouralism
facts.summary: Approach that dominated American political science in the 1950s and 1960s, studying observable behaviour with scientific, value-free methods.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Post-behaviouralism
facts.summary: Easton's call for relevance and action, bringing values and urgent social problems back into political science.
facts.note: Announced in Easton's 1969 presidential address to the American Political Science Association.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Duverger's law
facts.summary: The simple-majority single-ballot system tends to produce a two-party system; proportional representation tends to favour many parties.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Congress system
facts.summary: Kothari's account of Congress as a dominant party of consensus, with opposition parties acting as a margin of pressure.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Balance of power
facts.summary: Distribution of power among states such that no single state can dominate the rest; a core realist idea.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: National interest
facts.summary: The goals a state pursues abroad; Morgenthau's realism defines them as interest in terms of power.
facts.verified: books: Heywood; IGNOU Political Science Paper 2

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Security dilemma
facts.summary: Situation in which one state's measures for its own security make others feel less secure, leading to arms races.
facts.note: John Herz coined the term in 1950; Herbert Butterfield described the same idea in 1951.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Collective security
facts.summary: Arrangement in which all states agree to act together against any aggressor, as under the League Covenant and Chapter VII of the UN Charter.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Soft power
facts.summary: Ability to get what one wants through the attraction of culture, values and policies rather than coercion or payment.
facts.note: Coined in Nye's Bound to Lead (1990).

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Neorealism
facts.summary: Realism that explains state behaviour by the anarchic structure of the international system and the distribution of capabilities.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Constructivism
facts.summary: Approach holding that international structures are social, made of shared ideas, norms and identities rather than material power alone.
facts.note: Nicholas Onuf brought the term into IR in 1989; Wendt is its best-known theorist.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: World-systems theory
facts.summary: Sees one capitalist world-economy divided into core, semi-periphery and periphery, with surplus flowing to the core.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Dependency theory
facts.summary: Holds that developing countries stay underdeveloped because of unequal ties to the industrial core; associated with Prebisch and Andre Gunder Frank.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Functionalism
facts.summary: Mitrany's view that peace grows from international agencies built around shared practical tasks rather than political federation.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Clash of civilizations
facts.summary: Huntington's thesis that after the Cold War the main conflicts would run along cultural fault lines between civilizations.
facts.note: Foreign Affairs article 1993, expanded into a book in 1996.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Satyagraha
facts.summary: Gandhi's method of resisting injustice by truth and non-violence, aiming to convert the opponent through self-suffering.
facts.verified: books: Heywood; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Trusteeship
facts.summary: Gandhi's idea that the rich should hold their wealth in trust and use it for the good of society.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Radical humanism
facts.summary: Roy's philosophy that puts the free individual, reason and morality at the centre of politics instead of class or nation.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Basic structure doctrine
facts.summary: Supreme Court doctrine, laid down in Kesavananda Bharati, that Parliament can amend the Constitution but not destroy its basic structure.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Quasi-federal
facts.summary: Wheare's view of the Indian Constitution as a unitary state with subsidiary federal features rather than a federal state with unitary features.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Cooperative federalism
facts.summary: Austin's description of Indian federalism: a strong Centre that does not weaken the states but works together with them.
facts.note: Austin applied the term to India; it was in use earlier for other federations.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Non-alignment
facts.summary: India's policy of staying out of Cold War military blocs while keeping the freedom to judge each issue on its merits.
facts.note: The word is often credited to V. K. Krishna Menon.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Gujral Doctrine
facts.summary: Five principles under which India gives smaller neighbours what it can without asking for reciprocity, with non-interference and peaceful settlement.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Responsibility to Protect
facts.summary: Norm that each state must protect its people from genocide, war crimes, ethnic cleansing and crimes against humanity, and others may act if it fails.
facts.note: Proposed by the ICISS report in 2001; endorsed at the 2005 UN World Summit.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Founding of the Indian National Congress
facts.summary: First session met in Bombay under W. C. Bonnerjee with 72 delegates; A. O. Hume helped found it.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Non-Cooperation Movement
facts.summary: Gandhi's first all-India mass movement, joined with the Khilafat cause and called off after the violence at Chauri Chaura.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Civil Disobedience Movement
facts.summary: Mass breaking of colonial laws that began with Gandhi's Dandi March against the salt law in March 1930.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Quit India Movement
facts.summary: The AICC passed the Quit India resolution in Bombay with Gandhi's call of 'Do or Die'; leaders were arrested the next day.
facts.note: Resolution passed 8 August 1942; the arrests on 9 August are often given as the start.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Objectives Resolution
facts.summary: Resolution moved by Nehru in the Constituent Assembly that set out the Constitution's ideals and later became the basis of the Preamble.
facts.note: Moved on 13 December 1946, adopted on 22 January 1947.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Adoption of the Constitution of India
facts.summary: The Constituent Assembly adopted the Constitution, which came into force on 26 January 1950.
facts.note: Adopted 26 November 1949 (Constitution Day); in force 26 January 1950 (Republic Day).

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act
facts.summary: Gave constitutional status to panchayats, adding Part IX and the Eleventh Schedule and reserving one-third of seats for women.
facts.note: In force from 24 April 1993.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: 74th Constitutional Amendment Act
facts.summary: Gave constitutional status to urban local bodies, adding Part IX-A and the Twelfth Schedule.
facts.note: In force from 1 June 1993.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
facts.summary: Recommended democratic decentralisation through a three-tier panchayati raj of village, block and district bodies.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Sarkaria Commission
facts.summary: Commission on Centre-state relations that backed a strong Centre but urged sparing use of Article 356 and a permanent Inter-State Council.
facts.note: Set up in 1983; it reported in 1988.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Mandal Commission
facts.summary: Commission under B. P. Mandal that recommended 27 per cent reservation for Other Backward Classes in central government jobs.
facts.note: Set up 1979, reported 1980; the V. P. Singh government implemented it in 1990.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: NITI Aayog
facts.summary: Policy think tank that replaced the Planning Commission to promote cooperative federalism, without the power to allocate funds.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: National Human Rights Commission
facts.summary: Statutory body under the Protection of Human Rights Act of 1993 that inquires into violations of human rights.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Signing of the UN Charter
facts.summary: Fifty states, India among them, signed the Charter at the San Francisco Conference, founding the United Nations.
facts.note: In force 24 October 1945, now UN Day.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Universal Declaration of Human Rights
facts.summary: Adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris as a common standard of civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.
facts.verified: books: Baylis & Smith; IGNOU Political Science Paper 1

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Bretton Woods Conference
facts.summary: Conference of 44 Allied nations in New Hampshire that created the IMF and the World Bank and a system of fixed exchange rates.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Establishment of the World Trade Organization
facts.summary: The WTO replaced GATT as the body for global trade rules, created by the Marrakesh Agreement after the Uruguay Round.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Declaration on the Establishment of a New International Economic Order
facts.summary: UN General Assembly declaration, pushed by developing countries, for fairer trade, sovereignty over resources and reform of the world economy.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Panchsheel Agreement
facts.summary: India-China agreement on trade with the Tibet region whose preamble set out the five principles of peaceful coexistence.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Bandung Conference
facts.summary: Meeting of 29 Asian and African states in Indonesia that adopted ten principles and prepared the ground for non-alignment.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: First NAM Summit, Belgrade
facts.summary: First summit of the Non-Aligned Movement with 25 member states, led by Tito, Nehru, Nasser, Sukarno and Nkrumah.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons
facts.summary: Treaty that recognises five nuclear-weapon states; India refused to sign it as discriminatory.
facts.note: Opened for signature 1 July 1968; in force 5 March 1970.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Pokhran-I
facts.summary: India's first nuclear test, described by the government as a peaceful nuclear explosion.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Pokhran-II
facts.summary: Five nuclear tests on 11 and 13 May 1998, after which India declared itself a nuclear-weapon state.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: India's Nuclear Doctrine
facts.summary: Doctrine of credible minimum deterrence and no first use, with massive retaliation under civilian political control.
facts.note: A draft doctrine was released in August 1999.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: India-US Civil Nuclear Agreement
facts.summary: The signed 123 Agreement opened civil nuclear trade with India outside the NPT, after a Nuclear Suppliers Group waiver in September 2008.
facts.note: Began with the joint statement of 18 July 2005; books date the deal 2005 or 2008.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation
facts.summary: Twenty-year treaty signed months before the Bangladesh war, giving India Soviet support against the US-China-Pakistan alignment.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Simla Agreement
facts.summary: Indira Gandhi and Zulfikar Ali Bhutto agreed to settle disputes bilaterally and turned the Kashmir ceasefire line into the Line of Control.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Founding of SAARC
aliases: South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
facts.summary: Seven South Asian states founded SAARC at Dhaka; Afghanistan joined as the eighth member in 2007.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Act East Policy
facts.summary: Upgrade of the Look East Policy announced in 2014, adding security, connectivity and the wider Indo-Pacific to economic ties.
facts.note: Look East is usually dated 1991, under P. V. Narasimha Rao.

facts.subject: polsci
facts.name: Paris Agreement
facts.summary: Climate treaty under the UNFCCC in which every party sets nationally determined contributions to hold warming well below 2°C.
facts.note: In force from 4 November 2016.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Alexander von Humboldt
facts.summary: German naturalist and explorer who, with Carl Ritter, founded modern geography and studied nature as an interconnected whole through fieldwork in the Americas.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Friedrich Ratzel
facts.summary: German geographer who founded anthropogeography and modern political geography and is regarded as a founder of environmental determinism.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Ellen Churchill Semple
facts.summary: American geographer and student of Ratzel who spread environmental determinism in the English-speaking world.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Ellsworth Huntington
facts.summary: American geographer who argued that climate shapes human energy and the rise and fall of civilisations.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Paul Vidal de la Blache
facts.summary: French geographer and founder of the French school of human geography, whose regional studies of pays and genre de vie underlie possibilism.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Lucien Febvre
facts.summary: French historian of the Annales school who coined the term possibilism for the ideas of Vidal de la Blache.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Griffith Taylor
facts.summary: British-born Australian geographer who proposed neo-determinism as a middle path between determinism and possibilism.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Alfred Hettner
facts.summary: German geographer who defined geography as a chorological science of the differing character of areas and regions.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Richard Hartshorne
facts.summary: American geographer who defined geography as the study of areal differentiation and defended its regional and idiographic character.
facts.note: Husain's main text gives 1899-1992; his biographic notes print 1935-1992.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Fred K. Schaefer
facts.summary: German-born American geographer who attacked Hartshorne's exceptionalism and called for geography as a law-seeking spatial science.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Carl O. Sauer
facts.summary: American geographer of the Berkeley school who studied the cultural landscape and the human transformation of nature.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: David Harvey
facts.summary: British geographer who moved from positivist method in Explanation in Geography to Marxist and radical geography.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Yi-Fu Tuan
facts.summary: Chinese-born American geographer and leading figure of humanistic geography who wrote on space, place and the human bond with place.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Torsten Hägerstrand
facts.summary: Swedish geographer who modelled the spatial diffusion of innovations and founded time geography.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Halford Mackinder
facts.summary: British geographer and politician whose Heartland theory held that control of the interior of Eurasia is the key to world power.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Nicholas J. Spykman
facts.summary: Dutch-American political scientist who argued that the Rimland around Eurasia, not the Heartland, is the key to world power.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Walter Christaller
facts.summary: German geographer who developed central place theory from a study of settlements in southern Germany.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: August Lösch
facts.summary: German economist who extended central place ideas into a general theory of economic landscapes built of hexagonal market areas.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Johann Heinrich von Thünen
facts.summary: German landowner and economist who modelled concentric rings of agricultural land use around a single central market.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Alfred Weber
facts.summary: German economist and sociologist who developed the least-cost theory of industrial location.
facts.note: Brother of the sociologist Max Weber; not to be confused with him.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: W.W. Rostow
facts.summary: American economic historian who proposed five stages of economic growth from traditional society to the age of high mass consumption.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Gunnar Myrdal
facts.summary: Swedish economist who argued that market forces widen regional inequality through cumulative causation and backwash effects.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: François Perroux
facts.summary: French economist who proposed growth poles of propulsive industries in abstract economic space.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Albert O. Hirschman
facts.summary: German-born American economist who advocated unbalanced growth and described trickling-down and polarisation effects between regions.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: John Friedmann
facts.summary: Austrian-born American planner who proposed the core-periphery model of regional development.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Wilbur Zelinsky
facts.summary: American geographer who proposed the hypothesis of the mobility transition linking types of migration to stages of modernisation.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Thomas Robert Malthus
facts.summary: English clergyman and economist who argued that population tends to grow faster than the means of subsistence.
facts.note: Majid Husain prints 1760-1834 in both the text and the biographic notes.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Frank W. Notestein
facts.summary: American demographer who formulated the classic theory of demographic transition.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: E.G. Ravenstein
facts.summary: German-born British geographer who stated laws of migration from British census data.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Everett S. Lee
facts.summary: American demographer who explained migration through factors at origin and destination, intervening obstacles and personal factors.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Ester Boserup
facts.summary: Danish economist who argued against Malthus that population growth drives agricultural intensification.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Mark Jefferson
facts.summary: American geographer who described the primate city as a leading city disproportionately larger than the others.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: George Kingsley Zipf
facts.summary: American linguist who popularised the rank-size rule for the sizes of cities.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Ernest W. Burgess
facts.summary: American sociologist of the Chicago school who proposed the concentric zone model of urban structure.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Homer Hoyt
facts.summary: American land economist who proposed the sector model of urban residential land use.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Chauncy D. Harris
facts.summary: American geographer who with Edward Ullman proposed the multiple nuclei model of urban land use.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Patrick Geddes
facts.summary: Scottish biologist and town planner who coined the term conurbation and pioneered regional survey as the basis of planning.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Jean Gottmann
facts.summary: French geographer who used the term megalopolis for the urbanised northeastern seaboard of the United States.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: William Morris Davis
facts.summary: American geographer and geomorphologist who proposed the cycle of erosion in which landscapes pass through youth, maturity and old age.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Walther Penck
facts.summary: German geomorphologist who related landform development to the rate of uplift against the rate of denudation.
facts.note: Son of the glacial geomorphologist Albrecht Penck.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Lester C. King
facts.summary: South African geomorphologist who proposed pediplanation through the parallel retreat of slopes.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: James Hutton
facts.summary: Scottish geologist, often called the father of modern geology, who stated the principle of uniformitarianism.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Alfred Wegener
facts.summary: German meteorologist who proposed the theory of continental drift.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Harry H. Hess
facts.summary: American geologist who proposed sea-floor spreading from the mid-ocean ridges.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Arthur Holmes
facts.summary: British geologist who proposed convection currents in the mantle as the force that moves the continents.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Clarence Dutton
facts.summary: American geologist who coined the term isostasy.
facts.note: Husain gives 1841-1912; Savindra Singh gives 1843-1912.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Wladimir Köppen
facts.summary: German-Russian climatologist who devised the most widely used empirical classification of climates.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: C.W. Thornthwaite
facts.summary: American climatologist who classified climates by precipitation effectiveness and later by potential evapotranspiration.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Charles Darwin
facts.summary: English naturalist who, besides his theory of evolution, proposed the subsidence theory of coral reefs.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Arthur Tansley
facts.summary: British ecologist who coined the term ecosystem.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Derwent Whittlesey
facts.summary: American geographer who divided the world into major agricultural regions and introduced the idea of sequent occupance.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Anthropogeographie
facts.summary: Two-volume foundation of human geography that studies how the physical environment influences human societies.
facts.note: Volume 1 appeared in 1882 and volume 2 in 1891.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Influences of Geographic Environment
aliases: Influences of Geographic Environment on the Basis of Ratzel's System of Anthropo-Geography
facts.summary: Restates Ratzel's anthropogeography for English readers and opens with the claim that man is a product of the earth's surface.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Civilization and Climate
facts.summary: Argues that civilisation flourishes in stimulating climates and links human energy and progress to climate and weather.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Principles of Human Geography
facts.summary: Sets out human geography as the study of genres de vie and the relations between people and their milieu.
facts.note: Published after his death and edited by de Martonne; English translation 1926.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Nature of Geography
facts.summary: Surveys geographic thought and defines geography as the study of areal differentiation of the earth's surface.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Exceptionalism in Geography: A Methodological Examination
facts.summary: Paper attacking Hartshorne's view of geography as an exceptional discipline and calling for a spatial science that seeks laws.
facts.note: Published after Schaefer's death in 1953.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Geographical Pivot of History
facts.summary: Paper read to the Royal Geographical Society naming the pivot area of Eurasia as the seat of world power in the post-Columbian age.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Democratic Ideals and Reality
facts.summary: Renames the pivot area the Heartland and states the dictum linking East Europe, the Heartland and the World-Island.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Geography of the Peace
facts.summary: Posthumous book setting out the Rimland theory as a counter to Mackinder's Heartland.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Central Places in Southern Germany
facts.summary: Study of the towns of southern Germany that sets out central place theory.
facts.note: German original 1933; English translation 1966.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Economics of Location
facts.summary: Builds a general theory of location in which hexagonal market areas of many goods form an economic landscape.
facts.note: German original 1940; English translation 1954.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Isolated State
facts.summary: Models agricultural land use as concentric rings around a central city, set by economic rent and the cost of transport to market.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Theory of the Location of Industries
facts.summary: Sets out the least-cost theory of industrial location.
facts.note: German original 1909; English translation by C.J. Friedrich 1929.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Stages of Economic Growth
facts.summary: Proposes five stages: traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity and the age of high mass consumption.
facts.note: Subtitled A Non-Communist Manifesto.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Economic Theory and Under-developed Regions
facts.summary: Sets out circular and cumulative causation and the backwash and spread effects between rich and poor regions.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: An Essay on the Principle of Population
aliases: Essay on the Principle of Population
facts.summary: Argues that population grows geometrically and food arithmetically, so positive and preventive checks hold population to subsistence.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: A Theory of Migration
facts.summary: Explains migration by factors at origin and destination, intervening obstacles and personal factors.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Laws of Migration
facts.summary: States laws of migration such as most migrants moving short distances, by stages, towards great centres of commerce, each stream producing a counter-stream.
facts.note: Two papers: 1885 and 1889.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Conditions of Agricultural Growth
facts.summary: Argues against Malthus that population pressure leads farmers to intensify land use and adopt new techniques.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: The Origin of Continents and Oceans
aliases: Die Entstehung der Kontinente und Ozeane
facts.summary: Sets out continental drift with evidence from matching coastlines, fossils, rocks and past climates.
facts.note: Revised in several later editions.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Morphological Analysis of Land Forms
facts.summary: Relates the form of landscapes and slopes to the rates of crustal uplift and denudation.
facts.note: German original 1924 published after his death; English translation 1953.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Explanation in Geography
facts.summary: Sets out the philosophy and methods of positivist scientific geography during the quantitative revolution.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Social Justice and the City
facts.summary: Marks Harvey's turn from liberal to Marxist analysis of urban inequality and is a founding text of radical geography.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Topophilia
aliases: Topophilia: A Study of Environmental Perception
facts.summary: Studies the affective bond between people and place and is a founding text of humanistic geography.
facts.note: Husain's glossary says Tuan introduced the term to geography in 1961.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Environmental determinism
facts.summary: The view that the physical environment, especially climate and terrain, controls human activities and the course of history.
facts.note: Ratzel, Semple and Huntington are its main exponents.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Lebensraum
facts.summary: Ratzel's idea that the state, like an organism, needs living space and grows by expanding its territory.
facts.note: Later used by German geopolitics under Haushofer.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Possibilism
facts.summary: The view that nature offers possibilities and people choose among them, so human choice, not the environment, decides ways of life.
facts.note: Husain: advocated by Vidal de la Blache's school; Febvre postulated the term.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Genre de vie
facts.summary: Vidal's term for the way of life of a group, shaped by the physical, historical and social influences of its region.
facts.note: Husain makes it central to Vidal de la Blache's work; one passage says Febvre coined the term.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Neo-determinism
facts.summary: Taylor's view that people can speed, slow or stop a region's development but cannot change the course that nature sets.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Chorology
facts.summary: The view of geography as the study of the varying character of the earth's surface, area by area.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Areal differentiation
facts.summary: Hartshorne's definition of geography as the description and interpretation of the variable character of the earth's surface from place to place.
facts.note: Set out in The Nature of Geography (1939).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Quantitative revolution
facts.summary: The shift in geography in the 1950s and 1960s to statistical methods, models and the search for spatial laws.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Radical geography
facts.summary: A Marxist-influenced approach from the late 1960s that studies poverty, inequality and injustice as products of capitalist space.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Humanistic geography
facts.summary: An approach that studies human experience, perception and the meaning of place, against positivist spatial science.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Cultural landscape
facts.summary: Sauer's idea that a cultural group, working on the natural landscape over time, produces a cultural landscape.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Spatial diffusion of innovations
facts.summary: Hägerstrand's model of how innovations spread across space through personal contact, with adoption falling off with distance.
facts.note: Swedish original 1953; English translation 1967.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Heartland
facts.summary: Mackinder's idea that the interior of Eurasia, safe from sea power, is the pivot of world power.
facts.note: Called the Pivot Area in 1904; renamed the Heartland in Democratic Ideals and Reality (1919), with the dictum on East Europe and the World-Island.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Rimland
facts.summary: Spykman's idea that the coastal fringe around Eurasia holds the key to world power: who controls the Rimland rules Eurasia.
facts.note: Set out in The Geography of the Peace (1944).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Central place theory
facts.summary: Settlements serving their surrounding areas form a hierarchy of hexagonal market areas arranged by marketing (K=3), transport (K=4) or administrative (K=7) principles.
facts.note: German original 1933; English translation 1966.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Least-cost theory of industrial location
facts.summary: Industry locates where total transport and labour costs are least, found with the locational triangle, the material index and isodapanes.
facts.note: German original 1909; English translation 1929.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Cumulative causation
facts.summary: Myrdal's idea that a region's initial advantage is built on by market forces, so backwash effects outweigh spread effects and regional inequality widens.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Growth pole
facts.summary: Perroux's idea that growth starts at poles of propulsive industries and spreads unevenly through the economy.
facts.note: Some books date it to his 1950 paper on economic space; Boudeville gave it a regional meaning as growth centres.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Core-periphery model
facts.summary: Friedmann's model in which a dominant core region grows at the expense of a dependent periphery through stages of spatial development.
facts.note: Set out in Regional Development Policy: A Case Study of Venezuela (1966).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Trickling-down and polarisation effects
facts.summary: Hirschman's terms for growth spreading from developed to lagging regions (trickling down) and growth concentrating in the core (polarisation).
facts.note: Set out in The Strategy of Economic Development (1958).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Demographic transition
facts.summary: The model in which a population moves from high birth and death rates, through falling death rates, to low birth and death rates.
facts.note: First outlined by Warren Thompson in 1929; Notestein's 1945 version is the classic statement.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Mobility transition
facts.summary: Zelinsky's hypothesis that patterns of migration change in step with the stages of the demographic transition and modernisation.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Primate city
facts.summary: A country's leading city that is disproportionately larger than the next cities and expresses national life and feeling.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Rank-size rule
facts.summary: The population of the city of rank n equals the population of the largest city divided by n.
facts.note: First noted by Felix Auerbach in 1913; Zipf popularised it in 1949.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Concentric zone model
facts.summary: Burgess's model of a city growing outward in five concentric zones around the central business district.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Sector model
facts.summary: Hoyt's model in which residential areas grow outward in wedge-shaped sectors along transport routes from the centre.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Multiple nuclei model
facts.summary: Harris and Ullman's model in which a city grows around several separate nuclei rather than a single centre.
facts.note: Proposed jointly with Edward Ullman.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Conurbation
facts.summary: Geddes's term for a large urban region formed when growing towns merge into one continuous built-up area.
facts.note: Coined in Cities in Evolution (1915).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Megalopolis
facts.summary: Gottmann's term for a chain of merged metropolitan areas, first applied to the Boston-Washington seaboard.
facts.note: Set out in his book Megalopolis (1961).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Whittlesey's agricultural regions
aliases: Major Agricultural Regions of the Earth
facts.summary: Whittlesey's division of the world into thirteen major agricultural regions using five criteria such as crop and livestock association and intensity.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Cycle of erosion
facts.summary: Davis's model in which uplifted land is worn down through youth, maturity and old age to a peneplain, as a function of structure, process and stage.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Penck's model of landform development
facts.summary: Penck's model in which landforms depend on the ratio of uplift to denudation, with slopes developing by replacement from below.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Pediplanation
facts.summary: King's model in which scarps retreat parallel to themselves, leaving pediments that merge into a pediplain.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Uniformitarianism
aliases: present is the key to the past
facts.summary: The principle that the processes acting on the earth today also acted in the past.
facts.note: The phrase "the present is the key to the past" is often credited to Hutton but was coined later by Archibald Geikie.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Continental drift
facts.summary: Wegener's theory that the continents were once joined as Pangaea and have since drifted apart.
facts.note: First presented in 1912; set out in his book of 1915.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Sea-floor spreading
facts.summary: Hess's idea that new oceanic crust forms at mid-ocean ridges and moves outward to be consumed at ocean trenches.
facts.note: His paper History of Ocean Basins was published in 1962; Robert Dietz coined the term in 1961.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Convection current theory
facts.summary: Holmes's theory that convection currents in the mantle, driven by radioactive heat, move the continents.
facts.note: Proposed in the late 1920s.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Plate tectonics
facts.summary: The theory that the lithosphere is divided into rigid plates that move over the asthenosphere and interact at divergent, convergent and transform boundaries.
facts.note: Credited to McKenzie and Parker (1967) and to Morgan and Le Pichon (1968).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Isostasy
facts.summary: The state of balance in which crustal blocks stand on denser material below, higher land being compensated at depth.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Airy's concept of isostasy
facts.summary: G.B. Airy's view that crustal blocks of the same density sink to different depths, so mountains have deep roots.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Pratt's concept of isostasy
facts.summary: J.H. Pratt's view that crustal blocks reach a common level of compensation, higher blocks being of lower density.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Köppen's climatic classification
facts.summary: An empirical classification into five main groups, A to E, using temperature and precipitation values linked to natural vegetation.
facts.note: First published in 1900 and revised several times, notably in 1918 and 1936.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Thornthwaite's climatic classification
facts.summary: Classifications of climate by precipitation effectiveness and thermal efficiency, and later by potential evapotranspiration.
facts.note: Two schemes: 1931 and 1948.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Hadley cell
facts.summary: The thermally direct circulation in which air rises near the equator and sinks near 30 degrees latitude, feeding the trade winds.
facts.note: Named after George Hadley's 1735 explanation of the trade winds.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: El Niño-Southern Oscillation
facts.summary: The coupled ocean-atmosphere cycle in which El Niño warming of the eastern Pacific goes with a see-saw of pressure across the Pacific.
facts.note: Gilbert Walker identified and named the Southern Oscillation.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Bergeron-Findeisen process
facts.summary: Raindrops form when ice crystals in a cloud grow at the expense of supercooled water droplets, then fall and melt.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Thermal theory of the monsoon
facts.summary: Edmond Halley's explanation of the monsoon as a giant land and sea breeze caused by the unequal heating of land and sea.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Subsidence theory of coral reefs
facts.summary: Darwin's theory that fringing reefs become barrier reefs and then atolls as their volcanic island slowly subsides.
facts.note: Set out in The Structure and Distribution of Coral Reefs (1842).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Ecosystem
facts.summary: Tansley's term for a community of organisms together with its physical environment, functioning as one unit.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Damodar Valley Corporation
facts.summary: India's first multipurpose river valley project, set up by an Act of Parliament on the model of the Tennessee Valley Authority.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Planning Commission
facts.summary: Set up by a resolution of the Government of India to draw up five-year plans, with the Prime Minister as chairman.
facts.note: Khullar: constituted in 1950; another Khullar passage says set up by a Resolution in March 1951.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: First Five Year Plan
facts.summary: India's first five-year plan, which gave priority to agriculture, irrigation and power.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: National Development Council
facts.summary: Body of the Prime Minister, Union ministers and state chief ministers set up to approve five-year plans and bring the states into planning.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Community Development Programme
facts.summary: Launched on Gandhi Jayanti to develop rural areas block by block through people's participation.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: States Reorganisation Commission
facts.summary: Commission under Fazl Ali, set up in 1953, whose 1955 report led to the reorganisation of states largely on linguistic lines.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: States Reorganisation Act
facts.summary: Act that reorganised India into 14 states and 6 union territories, largely on linguistic lines.
facts.note: Came into force on 1 November 1956.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Indus Waters Treaty
facts.summary: Treaty brokered by the World Bank that gave India the eastern rivers (Ravi, Beas, Sutlej) and Pakistan the western rivers (Indus, Jhelum, Chenab).

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: High Yielding Varieties Programme
facts.summary: Programme that spread high-yielding seeds with fertiliser and irrigation and began the Green Revolution.
facts.note: Launched in 1966-67.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Drought Prone Areas Programme
facts.summary: Area development programme to reduce the effects of drought through watershed development, soil conservation and afforestation.
facts.note: Launched in 1973-74.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Command Area Development Programme
facts.summary: Programme to close the gap between irrigation potential created and used in the command areas of major and medium projects.
facts.note: Launched in 1974-75.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Tribal Sub-Plan
facts.summary: Strategy of earmarking plan funds for areas of tribal concentration, introduced in the Fifth Five Year Plan.
facts.note: Introduced in 1974-75.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: South Asian Association for Regional Cooperation
facts.summary: Regional association of South Asian countries founded at Dhaka with seven members; Afghanistan joined in 2007.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: 73rd Constitutional Amendment
facts.summary: Gave constitutional status to panchayats and made them units of local planning, the basis of decentralised planning.
facts.note: Passed in 1992; came into force on 24 April 1993.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: 74th Constitutional Amendment
facts.summary: Gave constitutional status to urban local bodies and provided for district and metropolitan planning committees.
facts.note: Passed in 1992; came into force on 1 June 1993.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: First Census of India
facts.summary: The first population census of India, conducted at different times in different parts of the country.
facts.note: Not synchronous; the first synchronous census was held in 1881.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Great Divide of 1921
facts.summary: The census year after which India's population has grown in every decade; 1911-21 is the only decade with a fall.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: National Population Policy 2000
facts.summary: Set goals of meeting contraceptive needs, reaching replacement-level fertility by 2010 and a stable population by 2045.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Bhuj earthquake
facts.summary: Earthquake centred near Bhuj in Kachchh, Gujarat, on Republic Day, one of the deadliest in India.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Indian Ocean tsunami
facts.summary: An earthquake off Sumatra set off a tsunami that struck the coasts of Tamil Nadu, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Disaster Management Act
facts.summary: Set up the National Disaster Management Authority under the Prime Minister, with state and district authorities.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: Jawaharlal Nehru National Urban Renewal Mission
facts.summary: Mission for urban infrastructure, basic services to the urban poor and governance reforms in selected cities.

facts.subject: geography
facts.name: NITI Aayog
facts.summary: Policy think tank of the Government of India that replaced the Planning Commission and works through cooperative federalism.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Woodrow Wilson
facts.summary: American scholar and later US President whose 1887 essay founded public administration as a separate field of study.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Frank J. Goodnow
facts.summary: American scholar who gave the politics-administration dichotomy its classic form in Politics and Administration (1900).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Leonard D. White
facts.summary: American scholar who wrote the first textbook of public administration (1926).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Frederick Winslow Taylor
facts.summary: American engineer known as the father of scientific management.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Henri Fayol
facts.summary: French mining engineer and manager who set out the elements and fourteen principles of management.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Luther Gulick
facts.summary: American classical theorist who coined POSDCORB and co-edited Papers on the Science of Administration with Lyndall Urwick.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Max Weber
facts.summary: German sociologist whose ideal type of bureaucracy is the starting point of organisation theory.
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Public Administration Paper 1; Mohit Bhattacharya

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Elton Mayo
facts.summary: Australian-born Harvard researcher whose work on the Hawthorne studies founded the human relations school.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Mary Parker Follett
facts.summary: American thinker on constructive conflict, power and the law of the situation; a bridge between classical and human relations thought.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Chester I. Barnard
facts.summary: American telephone executive who saw the organisation as a cooperative system and authority as resting on acceptance.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Herbert A. Simon
facts.summary: American behavioural scientist who made decision-making the core of administration; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1978.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: James G. March
facts.summary: American organisation theorist who co-wrote Organizations (1958) with Simon and the garbage can model.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Fred W. Riggs
facts.summary: American scholar of comparative and development administration, known for the prismatic-sala model.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Douglas McGregor
facts.summary: American management thinker known for Theory X and Theory Y.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Abraham Maslow
facts.summary: American psychologist known for the hierarchy of needs.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Frederick Herzberg
facts.summary: American psychologist known for the two-factor (motivation-hygiene) theory and job enrichment.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Chris Argyris
facts.summary: American organisation theorist known for the immaturity-maturity theory and for work on organisational learning.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Rensis Likert
facts.summary: American social psychologist known for participative management, the four systems of management and the linking pin.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Peter Drucker
facts.summary: Austrian-born management thinker who introduced management by objectives.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Dwight Waldo
facts.summary: American scholar who challenged value-free administration and sponsored the first Minnowbrook conference (1968).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Vincent Ostrom
facts.summary: American scholar who led the public choice approach in public administration and argued for democratic administration.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: William A. Niskanen
facts.summary: American economist who modelled bureaucrats as budget maximisers.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Christopher Hood
facts.summary: British scholar who coined the term New Public Management (1991).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: David Osborne
facts.summary: American writer who, with Ted Gaebler, set out entrepreneurial government in Reinventing Government (1992).
facts.verified: books: IGNOU Public Administration Paper 1; Mohit Bhattacharya

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Robert B. Denhardt
facts.summary: American scholar who, with Janet V. Denhardt, proposed the New Public Service as an alternative to New Public Management.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Charles E. Lindblom
facts.summary: American political scientist who set out incrementalism, or 'muddling through', in policy-making.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Yehezkel Dror
facts.summary: Israeli policy scientist who proposed the optimal model of policy-making.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Amitai Etzioni
facts.summary: Sociologist who proposed mixed scanning in decision-making and classified organisations by the type of compliance they use.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Harold D. Lasswell
facts.summary: American political scientist who founded the policy sciences and defined politics as who gets what, when, how.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: David Easton
facts.summary: Canadian-born American political scientist who gave the systems model of politics used in policy analysis.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: John W. Kingdon
facts.summary: American political scientist who gave the multiple streams model of agenda-setting.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Aaron Wildavsky
facts.summary: American scholar of budgeting and policy implementation, known for the incremental view of budgeting.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: A.V. Dicey
facts.summary: British jurist who defined the rule of law and contrasted it with French droit administratif.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: John M. Gaus
facts.summary: American scholar who introduced the ecological approach to public administration.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Robert K. Merton
facts.summary: American sociologist who analysed the dysfunctions of bureaucracy.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Gunnar Myrdal
facts.summary: Swedish economist who called South Asian states 'soft states'; Nobel Prize in Economics, 1974.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: David McClelland
facts.summary: American psychologist known for the theory of needs for achievement, power and affiliation.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Victor Vroom
facts.summary: Psychologist who gave the expectancy theory of motivation.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Fred E. Fiedler
facts.summary: Psychologist who gave the contingency model of leadership.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Robert R. Blake
facts.summary: American management theorist who developed the Managerial Grid with Jane Mouton.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Kautilya
facts.summary: Ancient Indian statesman and author of the Arthashastra, a treatise on statecraft and administration.
facts.note: Dates contested; usually placed in the Maurya period (c. 4th century BCE).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Paul H. Appleby
facts.summary: American administrator who reported on Indian public administration in 1953 and 1956.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Study of Administration
facts.summary: Argues for a science of administration separate from politics, borrowing efficient methods from Europe while keeping democratic control.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Politics and Administration
aliases: Politics and Administration: A Study in Government
facts.summary: Argues that politics expresses the will of the state and administration executes that will.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Introduction to the Study of Public Administration
facts.summary: The first textbook of public administration; treats administration as management, with efficiency as its aim.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Principles of Scientific Management
facts.summary: Argues that scientific study of each task, not rule of thumb, raises output and serves both workers and management.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: General and Industrial Management
facts.summary: Sets out the five elements of management and fourteen principles of administration.
facts.note: French original 1916; English translations 1929 and 1949.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Papers on the Science of Administration
facts.summary: Classical essays prepared for the Brownlow Committee, including Gulick's 'Notes on the Theory of Organization', which set out POSDCORB.
facts.note: Co-edited by Gulick and Lyndall Urwick.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Economy and Society
facts.summary: Weber's posthumous treatise on economy, authority and society; contains his analysis of legitimate authority and bureaucracy.
facts.note: German original 1922 (posthumous); English editions 1947 (partial) and 1968 (full).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization
aliases: Human Problems of an Industrial Civilization
facts.summary: Uses the Hawthorne findings to argue that workers' social and emotional needs shape output more than pay and physical conditions.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Dynamic Administration
aliases: Dynamic Administration: The Collected Papers of Mary Parker Follett
facts.summary: Posthumous collection of Follett's papers on constructive conflict, the giving of orders, power, control and coordination.
facts.note: Edited by Metcalf and Urwick; editions are dated 1940 to 1942.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Functions of the Executive
facts.summary: Treats the organisation as a cooperative system that the executive keeps in balance through communication, incentives and accepted authority.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Proverbs of Administration
facts.summary: Article arguing that the classical principles of administration come in contradictory pairs, like proverbs, and so cannot guide action.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Administrative Behavior
aliases: Administrative Behavior: A Study of Decision-Making Processes in Administrative Organization
facts.summary: Makes decision-making the heart of administration, studying it through factual and value premises and the limits of rationality.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Ecology of Public Administration
facts.summary: Lectures arguing that administration can be understood only within its social, economic, political and cultural setting.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Administration in Developing Countries: The Theory of Prismatic Society
facts.summary: Sets out the prismatic society and its sala administration, marked by heterogeneity, formalism and overlapping.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Human Side of Enterprise
facts.summary: Contrasts Theory X and Theory Y assumptions about people at work and argues for management by integration and self-control.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Personality and Organization
facts.summary: Argues that formal organisation keeps workers passive and dependent, in conflict with the needs of the mature adult personality.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: New Patterns of Management
facts.summary: Draws on Michigan research to show that supportive, group-based participative management gives better results.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Administrative State
facts.summary: Shows that American public administration theory rests on political values, challenging the claim of value-free efficiency.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Intellectual Crisis in American Public Administration
aliases: Intellectual Crisis in American Public Administration
facts.summary: Argues that the Wilson-Weber theory of bureaucracy has failed and proposes democratic administration built on public choice.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Bureaucracy and Representative Government
facts.summary: Models bureaucrats as budget maximisers who push their agencies' budgets and output beyond what voters want.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Reinventing Government
aliases: Reinventing Government: How the Entrepreneurial Spirit Is Transforming the Public Sector
facts.summary: Sets out ten principles of entrepreneurial government, such as steering rather than rowing and meeting the needs of the customer.
facts.note: Co-written by David Osborne and Ted Gaebler.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Science of 'Muddling Through'
facts.summary: Argues that policy makers move by successive limited comparisons from existing policy, not by comprehensive rational analysis.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Policy Sciences
aliases: Policy Sciences: Recent Developments in Scope and Method
facts.summary: Volume containing Lasswell's essay 'The Policy Orientation', which launched the policy sciences as a problem-oriented, multi-disciplinary field.
facts.note: Edited with Daniel Lerner.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: A Systems Analysis of Political Life
facts.summary: Treats the political system as turning environmental inputs of demands and supports into authoritative outputs, with feedback.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: The Politics of the Budgetary Process
facts.summary: Shows that budgeting is incremental and political: each budget starts from last year's base and changes a little through bargaining.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Implementation: How Great Expectations in Washington Are Dashed in Oakland
facts.summary: Study of a federal jobs programme in Oakland showing how many clearance points and actors defeat policy implementation.
facts.note: Co-written by Jeffrey Pressman and Aaron Wildavsky.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution
facts.summary: Sets out parliamentary sovereignty and the rule of law, and holds that England has no separate administrative law like France's.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Arthashastra
facts.summary: Treatise on statecraft covering the king, ministers, officials, revenue, espionage, law and foreign policy.
facts.note: Date contested (often placed c. 4th century BCE); rediscovered by R. Shamasastry, who published it in 1909.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Public Administration in India: Report of a Survey
facts.summary: Survey that ranked India's government among the most advanced, and led to the O&M Division and the Indian Institute of Public Administration (1954).
facts.note: A second Appleby report on public enterprises followed in 1956.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Politics-administration dichotomy
facts.summary: The view that politics decides policy and administration carries it out, so administration can be a neutral, separate field.
facts.note: Wilson raised it in 1887; Goodnow gave it its classic form in 1900.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: POSDCORB
facts.summary: Gulick's acronym for the chief executive's work: planning, organising, staffing, directing, co-ordinating, reporting and budgeting.
facts.note: Coined by Gulick (not Urwick); it builds on Fayol's elements of management.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Scientific management
facts.summary: Taylor's method of finding the one best way of work through time study, standard tools and methods, scientific selection and training, and incentive pay.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Fourteen principles of management
facts.summary: Fayol's principles, including division of work, authority, discipline, unity of command, unity of direction, scalar chain and esprit de corps.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Ideal type of bureaucracy
facts.summary: Weber's model of rational administration: hierarchy, rules, specialised offices, written files, impersonality and full-time officials appointed on merit.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Types of legitimate authority
facts.summary: Weber's three types of authority: traditional, charismatic and legal-rational; bureaucracy is the purest form of legal-rational authority.
facts.verified: books: D. Ravindra Prasad; IGNOU Public Administration Paper 1

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Human relations school
facts.summary: Approach holding that informal groups, morale and workers' social needs shape output more than physical conditions and pay.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Constructive conflict
facts.summary: Follett's view that conflict is best settled by integration, a solution meeting both sides' desires, rather than by domination or compromise.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Acceptance theory of authority
facts.summary: Barnard's view that authority lies in the subordinate's acceptance of an order, not in the position of the person who gives it.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Zone of indifference
facts.summary: The range of orders a subordinate accepts without questioning them; Simon later called it the zone of acceptance.
facts.note: Barnard's term; Simon's 'zone of acceptance' is the same idea.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Bounded rationality
facts.summary: Simon's idea that limits of information, time and mental capacity stop decision-makers from finding the best choice.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Satisficing
facts.summary: Choosing the first option that is good enough rather than the best; Simon's 'administrative man' satisfices while 'economic man' maximises.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Fact-value dichotomy
facts.summary: Simon's split between factual premises, which can be tested, and value premises, which cannot; he used it in place of the politics-administration dichotomy.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Prismatic society
facts.summary: Riggs's model of a transitional society between fused (traditional) and diffracted (modern) types, where old and new structures coexist.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Sala model
facts.summary: Riggs's name for administration in a prismatic society, where formal rules coexist with family, caste and other particular ties.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Theory X and Theory Y
facts.summary: Theory X assumes people dislike work and must be controlled; Theory Y assumes they can enjoy work, seek responsibility and direct themselves.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Hierarchy of needs
facts.summary: Maslow's five levels of need: physiological, safety, social, esteem and self-actualisation; a need that is met stops motivating.
facts.note: First set out in 1943; developed in Motivation and Personality (1954).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Two-factor theory
facts.summary: Herzberg's theory that hygiene factors such as pay and conditions only prevent dissatisfaction, while motivators such as achievement and recognition motivate.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Immaturity-maturity theory
facts.summary: Argyris's view that people grow from passive, dependent immaturity to active, independent maturity, but formal organisations keep them immature.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Four systems of management
facts.summary: Likert's scale from exploitative-authoritative (System 1) through benevolent-authoritative and consultative to participative group (System 4), the most effective.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Management by objectives
facts.summary: Managers and staff agree clear objectives together, and performance is reviewed against them.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: New Public Administration
facts.summary: Movement from the 1968 Minnowbrook conference stressing relevance, values, social equity, change and client focus over efficiency alone.
facts.note: Linked with Waldo, Marini and Frederickson rather than with one founder.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Public choice approach
facts.summary: Applies economics' self-interested chooser to government, favouring many overlapping agencies, competition and citizen choice over one large hierarchy.
facts.note: IGNOU names Vincent Ostrom a protagonist of the approach.

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: New Public Management
facts.summary: Reform model bringing private-sector methods into government: performance targets, output control, markets, contracting out and separate agencies.
facts.note: Term coined by Christopher Hood in 'A Public Management for All Seasons?' (1991).

facts.subject: pub-admin
facts.name: Entrepreneurial government
